verdict_reasoning: No surviving objection questions the goal or the parse-analysis design. The one surviving objection, standards-compat-1, is fixable: the patch accepts BY on either side of OVERRIDING and BY POSITION with DEFAULT VALUES, and nobody has checked these forms against the draft standard text. A committer who knows the grammar and the standard would need to sign off on the released syntax.

brief.title: Add insert ... by name to match source columns by name
brief.problem: Positional insert ... select breaks or puts data in the wrong column when the source query lists columns in a different order than the target. The author cites the forthcoming SQL standard, which accepted BY NAME for INSERT, and similar syntax in DuckDB and Oracle 23ai.
brief.proposed_design: A new optional clause `BY { NAME | POSITION }` sits before OVERRIDING and the source, and BY POSITION is the default. Parse analysis resolves BY NAME by reordering the target column and attribute-number lists to match the source columns, so the query tree is an ordinary positional insert and rule and view deparsing need no change.
user_visible_surface: SQL syntax: `insert into t [ (cols) ] by { name | position } [ overriding ... ] query`, accepted on either side of OVERRIDING.
New errors for unknown source names, duplicate matches, bare VALUES or DEFAULT VALUES with BY NAME, and subfield or array-element targets.
psql tab completion for BY NAME and BY POSITION (added in v2).
author_claims: The SQL draft standard accepted the feature, and DuckDB and Oracle 23ai implement the same core behavior.
Target columns that the source does not name get their default values, as if left out of the column list.
Resolving BY NAME in parse analysis means no rule or view deparsing changes are needed.
`select *` and named VALUES wrapped in a subquery work with BY NAME, and v2 adds tests for them.
brief.thread_state: Four reviewers tested the patch and report that it works, and Andreas Karlsson confirms the standard's semantics for an explicit column list. v2 addressed Vaibhav Dalvi's review, and he left two small items: tab completion after BY NAME, and a regression test for `by name table other_table`.
unclear: No one has checked the patch against the draft standard text, and Jim Jones said he would try to get it.
The material does not say whether name matching follows identifier case rules, for example a quoted alias against an unquoted column.
The material does not say how BY NAME interacts with ON CONFLICT, RETURNING, generated columns or identity columns.
No one has answered the author's question on keeping old insert_rest rules and adding insert_by_options only for the new forms.
The material does not say whether BY NAME is planned for other commands, such as union by name or merge.

prior_attempts.title: Corresponding by clause for set operation
prior_attempts.quote: The main thing that's scaring me off is a realization that there are a *lot* of places that assume that the output columns of a set operation are one-for-one with the columns of the inputs.
prior_attempts.reason: After Pavel Stehule marked it ready for committer, Tom Lane found that much code assumes set operation output columns map one-for-one to input columns, and the patch had not changed that code. As a result, qual pushdown into a view fails with "wrong number of tlist entries", UNION ALL appendrel conversion returns columns in the wrong order, and WITH RECURSIVE fails. ruleutils.c also reverse-lists views wrongly and does not track column renames. David Steele returned the entry because no committable patch was likely before the commitfest ended.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P4 matched set-operation inputs by name and broke code that assumes set-operation outputs map one-for-one to inputs. This proposal resolves BY NAME in parse analysis into an ordinary positional insert with a reordered target column list, a form INSERT already supports.

objections.title: Grammar commitments go beyond the unverified draft standard text
objections.failure_scenario: The published standard fixes BY NAME to one position relative to OVERRIDING, or does not allow BY POSITION with DEFAULT VALUES. Postgres has already released both orders and the no-op form. It must then keep the non-standard spellings for compatibility, or break user scripts that rely on them.
objections.argument: No one has checked the patch against the draft text. Jim Jones said he would try to get it (message #7), and Andreas Karlsson confirmed only the explicit column list case (messages #4 and #5). The patch accepts the clause on either side of OVERRIDING and accepts BY POSITION with DEFAULT VALUES. The thread does not say whether the draft allows either form. Syntax extensions are hard to remove once released, so a committer would likely want each accepted form tied to the draft grammar before commit.
objections.author_must_show: Which of the accepted forms, both OVERRIDING orders and BY POSITION with DEFAULT VALUES, does the draft standard grammar allow?

critic.reasoning: The thread confirms only the explicit column list case against the accepted change proposal. Nobody has checked the two OVERRIDING orders or BY POSITION with DEFAULT VALUES against the draft, and a released spelling is hard to remove.

refuted.title: Syntax ships before the standard text is final or checked
refuted.failure_scenario: Postgres 20 ships INSERT ... BY NAME, and applications start to depend on its details. The published standard then differs on one point, such as a source column that matches no target, case folding of names, or where BY sits relative to OVERRIDING. Postgres must then keep a non-standard behaviour forever or break those applications in a later major release.
refuted.argument: Message #4 says the feature is "technically not yet in the standard" and is only expected to be. No one in the thread has read the draft text; Jim Jones planned to get it (message #7), and nothing after that reports a check. Andreas Karlsson confirmed one case from memory of the meeting, the explicit column list. Other choices are the patch's own, such as accepting BY on either side of OVERRIDING and treating BY POSITION as a no-op with DEFAULT VALUES, and they become permanent syntax once released.
refuted.author_must_show: Has someone compared each behaviour in v2 against the accepted change proposal text, and which choices does that text leave to the implementation?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which names the specific forms that go beyond what the thread confirmed. The parts unique to this objection, case folding and unmatched source columns, have no shown conflict with the draft.

touch_points.reason: The patch changes the raw InsertStmt node in parsenodes.h, which extensions that inspect parse trees can see.

questions: Which of the accepted forms, both OVERRIDING orders and BY POSITION with DEFAULT VALUES, does the draft standard grammar allow?
Does name matching follow identifier case rules, for example a quoted source alias `"C1"` against an unquoted target column c1?
How does BY NAME behave with generated columns, identity columns, ON CONFLICT and RETURNING?
Without a target column list, does the patch check insert privilege only on the columns that the source query names?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows gram.y and parse analysis of INSERT, and who can read the draft SQL standard text. The visible thread and the CommitFest entry show no such committer taking part.
committability.liability: The owner signs for every accepted spelling of the clause for as long as Postgres keeps INSERT syntax compatible, including any form the published standard later does not allow.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v2 in message #12 in response to Vaibhav Dalvi's review, which shows follow-up during review.

priority.reason: The patch is about 29 KiB, touches only the parser, docs, psql completion and tests, and resolves to an ordinary positional insert. The open point is a check of the accepted forms against the draft standard, which does not need a redesign.

precedents_retrieved.title: [PROPOSAL] : Disallow use of empty column name in (column_name '') in ALTER or CREATE of foreign table.
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch makes postgres_fdw's validator reject empty values for the column_name, schema_name and table_name options in create or alter foreign table. Today an empty column_name is accepted, and the remote query then fails with a zero-length identifier error.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane judged that the check did not add enough ease-of-use to justify the extra code, and he compared an empty name to a misspelled remote name, which cannot be checked either. Robert Haas pointed out that existing foreign tables with empty values would then fail pg_dump or pg_upgrade. Nobody argued for the patch after Tom voted against it, so Robert marked it Rejected.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I was down on it to start with, on the grounds that it wasn't adding enough ease-of-use to justify even a relatively small amount of added code.

precedents_retrieved.title: Permute underscore separated components of columns before fuzzy matching
precedents_retrieved.summary: Extend the fuzzy column-name matching behind the "Perhaps you meant" hint so that it also checks permutations of up to three underscore-separated words. A swap of two words costs the same as one mistyped character, and the permutation is skipped when the typed name has more than six underscores.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that the patch adds opaque, almost undocumented code to the matching function, and he doubted that many users want this behavior. He also noted that adjacent underscores and leading or trailing underscores are not handled well. The visible messages show no reply from the author after this review, and the entry was returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
However, we *do*
need to be concerned about its maintainability, and I think the patch
falls down badly there: it adds a chunk of very opaque and essentially
undocumented code, that people will need to reverse-engineer anytime
they are studying this function.

precedents_retrieved.title: INSERT SELECT: BulkInsertState and table_multi_insert
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make INSERT, including INSERT SELECT and INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, use a BulkInsertState ring buffer as COPY does, so data loaders do not leave many dirty buffers in shared buffers. Later versions added a GUC to opt in, and switched to table_multi_insert after a set number of tuples.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The thread stalled. The multi-insert part became complex: it cannot handle volatile column defaults, and the author proposed leaving it to the separate "New Table Access Methods for Multi and Single Inserts" patch. The author split off the simple BulkInsertState patch and said to close the entry if no one was interested in it alone. No reviewer took that patch up, so the commitfest manager proposed closing it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Since the thread has stalled, maybe that's the best course of action here.

precedents_retrieved.title: Corresponding by clause for set operation
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the SQL-standard CORRESPONDING [BY (column list)] clause to UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT, so set operations match input columns by name. The parser computes the common or listed columns, and projection below the set operation reorders and trims each input to that list.
precedents_retrieved.objection: After Pavel Stehule marked it ready for committer, Tom Lane found that much code assumes set operation output columns map one-for-one to input columns, and the patch had not changed that code. As a result, qual pushdown into a view fails with "wrong number of tlist entries", UNION ALL appendrel conversion returns columns in the wrong order, and WITH RECURSIVE fails. ruleutils.c also reverse-lists views wrongly and does not track column renames. David Steele returned the entry because no committable patch was likely before the commitfest ended.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The main thing that's scaring me off is a realization that there are a *lot* of places that assume that the output columns of a set operation are one-for-one with the columns of the inputs.

precedents_retrieved.title: Parallel INSERT (INTO ... SELECT ...)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set allows parallel execution of both the INSERT and the SELECT parts of "INSERT INTO ... SELECT ...", with workers inserting tuples themselves; where parallel insert is unsafe (for example foreign keys or ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE), only the SELECT part is parallelised. It changes the planner, executor and parallel-worker code, adds parallel-safety checks on the target table (including partitions, triggers and domains), and adds a GUC and a reloption to control the feature.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Parts of the work, "Parallel SELECT for INSERT" and the related GUC/reloption, were committed during the thread. The remaining patches, which add the parallel INSERT functionality itself, were marked Returned with Feedback because of feedback given on pgsql-committers, which said a lot of work remained. The visible messages do not show the content of that feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
There is a lot of work
to do for this patch as per the feedback given on pgsql-committers
[1].

precedents_retrieved.title: Improving default column names/aliases of subscript text expressions
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes the default column name for a subscript expression with a string-literal subscript, such as data['a'] on jsonb, to the subscript value instead of the base column name. A later POC derives the name from the transformed expression and leaves room for type-specific hooks, so subscript implementations could supply their own default alias.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected that changing default column names breaks existing queries, and that a GUC to switch the behavior would change query semantics. He was not convinced the new names were better, preferring names like "data_a" if anything changed. He called the transformed-expression POC a single-purpose kluge and suggested that extensible field selection would serve the author's use case better.

precedents_retrieved.title: Mention column name in error messages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the target column name to errors raised when a value cannot be coerced to a column's type in INSERT or ALTER COLUMN, for example "value too long for type character varying(4)". After review, the first version, which changed datatype input functions, was reworked to use an error context callback in the parser.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund reviewed the patch and asked for code cleanups and tests, since the patch had none. The author did not reply, and Michael Paquier marked it returned with feedback two months after that review because the comments had not been addressed.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
Patch is marked as returned with feedback, it has been two months
since the last review, and comments have not been addressed.

precedents_retrieved.title: Mention column name in error messages
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds the target column name and type to errors raised when a value is coerced into an insert or update column, such as "value too long for type character varying(4)". After review it used an error context callback set up during parse analysis of assigned expressions instead of changing datatype input functions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane found that the callback only covers errors raised during parse analysis or constant folding, not run-time errors from non-constant expressions, and covering those would need executor changes with a likely performance cost. He argued that partial coverage would mislead users and that the cases it handles already have error cursor information. He proposed extending error cursor support into execution instead, and Michael Paquier returned the patch with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
If it isn't,
we'd be best off to reject this patch rather than create an expectation
among users that such context should be there.

precedents_retrieved.title: In INSERT/UPDATE, use the table's real tuple descriptor as target.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
In INSERT/UPDATE, use the table's real tuple descriptor as target.
Reverted commit(s): Fix corner case for a BEFORE ROW UPDATE trigger returning OLD.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Previously, ExecInitModifyTable relied on ExecInitJunkFilter,
and thence ExecCleanTypeFromTL, to build the target descriptor from
the query tlist.  While we just checked (in ExecCheckPlanOutput)
that the tlist produces compatible output, this is not a great
substitute for the relation's actual tuple descriptor that's
available from the relcache.  For one thing, dropped columns will
not be correctly marked attisdropped; it's a bit surprising that
we've gotten away with that this long.  But the real reason for
being concerned with this is that using the table's descriptor means
that the slot will have correct attrmissing data, allowing us to
revert the klugy fix of commit ba9f18abd.  (This commit undoes
that one's changes in trigger.c, but keeps the new test case.)
Thus we can solve the bogus-trigger-tuple problem with fewer cycles
rather than more.

No back-patch, since this doesn't fix any additional bug, and it
seems somewhat more likely to have unforeseen side effects than
ba9f18abd's narrow fix.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert applying column aliases to the output of whole-row Vars.
Reverted commit(s): Ensure that RowExprs and whole-row Vars produce the expected column names.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
In commit bf7ca1587, I had the bright idea that we could make the
result of a whole-row Var (that is, foo.*) track any column aliases
that had been applied to the FROM entry the Var refers to.  However,
that's not terribly logically consistent, because now the output of
the Var is no longer of the named composite type that the Var claims
to emit.  bf7ca1587 tried to handle that by changing the output
tuple values to be labeled with a blessed RECORD type, but that's
really pretty disastrous: we can wind up storing such tuples onto
disk, whereupon they're not readable by other sessions.

The only practical fix I can see is to give up on what bf7ca1587
tried to do, and say that the column names of tuples produced by
a whole-row Var are always those of the underlying named composite
type, query aliases or no.  While this introduces some inconsistencies,
it removes others, so it's not that awful in the abstract.  What *is*
kind of awful is to make such a behavioral change in a back-patched
bug fix.  But corrupt data is worse, so back-patched it will be.

(A workaround available to anyone who's unhappy about this is to
introduce an extra level of sub-SELECT, so that the whole-row Var is
referring to the sub-SELECT's output and not to a named table type.
Then the Var is of type RECORD to begin with and there's no issue.)

Per report from Miles Delahunty.  The faulty commit dates to 9.5,
so back-patch to all supported branches.

roaster_notes.note: The only related precedent is P4, and its recorded reason does not apply. It failed because set-operation code assumes outputs map one-for-one to inputs, and this patch leaves set operations unchanged and yields an ordinary insert with a reordered column list. The thread cites no earlier attempt at INSERT BY NAME, and message #1 says the author found none.

Other compatibility points hold. BY NAME is opt-in, so existing statements keep their meaning. Resolution in parse analysis means deparsed rules and dumps show a plain positional insert that older servers accept. The INSERT alias needs AS, so no grammar ambiguity is visible.

The proposal has no persistent or cross-node state for this angle to object to. BY NAME is resolved in parse analysis into an ordinary positional column mapping, so the stored Query tree, pg_rewrite contents, ruleutils deparsing, WAL, on-disk format, replication and the wire protocol are unchanged. The parsenodes.h change touches only the raw InsertStmt, which is never stored. A rule or SQL function body that uses BY NAME is stored and dumped in its resolved positional form, the same way a view stores an expanded select *. Without the code, this angle cannot confirm that the Query node itself gains no new field, which would need a catversion bump.

The proposal has no security or privilege aspect worth objecting to. BY NAME is resolved in parse analysis into an ordinary positional insert, so column insert privileges, RLS, triggers and rules apply as they do for an explicit column list. Error texts name only target columns, which the catalogs already expose. One point needs the code to confirm: without a column list, insert privilege should be checked only on matched columns.

Other maintenance concerns do not apply. BY NAME is resolved in parse analysis, adds no executor, planner, catalog or ABI cost, and avoids the column-mapping problem that stopped CORRESPONDING [P4]. No committer has engaged yet, but that is a committability point and not a flaw in the design.

The existing alternative is an explicit target column list, `insert into t (b, a) select ...`, which already reorders columns, so BY NAME adds convenience and no new capability. I would not send that objection, because the clause is accepted for the next SQL standard, DuckDB and Oracle 23ai already have it, and it resolves to an ordinary positional insert. No extension or hook could give the same grammar. [P4] is about set operations, and its reason, that output columns stop mapping one-for-one to input columns, does not apply here.

The material shows enough demand for a syntax feature whose cost falls only on its users. The SQL committee accepted BY NAME for INSERT (message #4), DuckDB and Oracle 23ai ship it (message #1), and four independent reviewers tested it. BY POSITION stays the default, and BY NAME resolves in parse analysis to an ordinary positional insert, so non-users pay nothing on the hot path. The workaround is an explicit column list in the right order, which helps a little but not when the source is `select *` from a table with a different column order. Questions about the standard text and identifier case rules belong to other angles.
